Decomposition of Changes in Impoverishment Estimates

Poverty headcount and impoverishment rates dynamics

World Bank–WHO GMR Technical Meeting

Geneva, November 2026

Motivation

Declining trends in global financial hardship and in global poverty reduction

Between 2000 and 2022, poverty at the societal poverty line fell from 42.6% to 25.1% of the world population and financial hardship (SDG 3.8.2, 2025 definition) from 33.6% to 26.0%, almost entirely through the impoverishing component (28.9% → 20.4%); large but non‑impoverishing OOP rose (4.6% → 5.6%) (WHO and World Bank 2025).

Interpretation

Story A — Poverty reduction is driving most of the changes in declining impoverishment

  • Any poor household with OOP > 0 counts as impoverished: fewer poor, fewer impoverished.
  • Financial protection may not have improved at all.

Story B — Health systems are better at providing financial protection

  • Prepaid, pooled financing expanded; user fees were removed.
  • Fewer poor pay at the point of use; fewer are pushed below the line.

In the 2025 GMR, we lean towards A: “the decline in impoverishing OOP health spending was driven by global poverty reduction rather than by health systems’ ability to provide better financial protection to the poor” (WHO and World Bank 2025). For the next GMR, we want to quantify this more precisely.

Objectives

  1. Partition the change in impoverishing OOP, ΔI\Delta I, into a poverty component and a financial‑protection component, with no residual.
  2. Implement the decomposition at two levels:
    • (i) Macro-level: from country‑year datapoints already published (poverty headcounts; impoverishment components).
    • (ii) Micro-level: from household survey data with total consumption, OOP and a poverty line.
  3. Assess how the dynamics of poverty affected the dynamics of impoverishment.

Measurement background

SDG 3.8.2 indicator revision

Poverty measurement

Per capita consumption xix_i (gross of OOP) and the societal poverty line (Jolliffe and Prydz 2021):

ztSPL=max⁡{2.15,1.15+0.5medt(x−m)}(2017 PPP, per day),Pt=1N∑i𝟏[xi<zt] z_t^{SPL}=\max\{2.15,\; 1.15+0.5\,\mathrm{med}_t(x-m)\}\ \ \text{(2017 PPP, per day)},\qquad P_t=\frac1N\sum_i\mathbf 1[x_i<z_t]

Financial hardship measurement

OOP mim_i exceeding 40% of the discretionary budget xi−ztx_i-z_t, in two mutually exclusive components (WHO and World Bank 2025):

FHt=1N∑i𝟏[mi>0.4(xi−zt),mi>0]=It+Lt FH_t=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \mathbf{1}\big[m_i>0.4\,(x_i-z_t),\; m_i>0\big]=I_t+L_t

Global estimates Condition 2000 2022
SPL poverty headcount, PtP_t xi<ztx_i<z_t 42.6% 25.1%
Financial hardship, FHt=It+LtFH_t=I_t+L_t 33.6% 26.0%
Impoverishing OOP, ItI_t xi−mi<zt,mi>0x_i-m_i<z_t,\ m_i>0 (further pushed + pushed) 28.9% 20.4%
Large, non‑impoverishing OOP, LtL_t 0.4(xi−zt)<mi<xi−zt0.4(x_i-z_t)<m_i<x_i-z_t 4.6% 5.6%

Sources: WHO & World Bank, 2025 Global Monitoring Report; poverty from the World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform.

Poverty and health impoverishment

  • “In poverty”: Foster–Greer–Thorbecke (Foster et al. 1984): Pα(y;z)=1N∑i(z−yiz)α𝟏[yi<z] P_\alpha(y;z)=\frac1N\sum_i\left(\frac{z-y_i}{z}\right)^{\alpha}\mathbf 1[y_i<z]

With α=0\alpha=0 we have the poverty headcount: P0(x;zt)=1N∑i𝟏[xi<zt]=PtP_0(x;z_t)=\frac1N\sum_i\mathbf 1[x_i<z_t]=P_t.

  • “Pushed into poverty” is the headcount difference ΔP0=P0(x−m;z)⏟net of OOP−P0(x;z)⏟gross of OOP\Delta P_0=\underbrace{P_0(x-m;z)}_{\text{net of OOP}}-\underbrace{P_0(x;z)}_{\text{gross of OOP}} (Wagstaff and Doorslaer 2003).
  • “Further pushed” are the poor with mi>0m_i>0 (WHO and World Bank 2025): invisible to ΔP0\Delta P_0, visible in the gap difference ΔP1\Delta P_1.
  • The impoverishing component of FH can therefore be rewritten as the poverty headcount on consumption net of OOP, restricted to people with positive OOP — it counts both the further pushed and the pushed: It=1N∑i𝟏[xi−mi<zt]𝟏[mi>0]=Pr⁡(x<zt,m>0)⏟further pushed+Pr⁡(x≥zt,x−m<zt)⏟pushed. I_t=\frac1N\sum_i \mathbf 1[x_i-m_i<z_t]\,\mathbf 1[m_i>0] =\underbrace{\Pr(x<z_t,\ m>0)}_{\text{further pushed}}+\underbrace{\Pr(x\ge z_t,\ x-m<z_t)}_{\text{pushed}}.

Intuition

Poverty and health impoverishment

  • Total impoverishment ItI_t can also be rewritten as a weighted average of two conditional hardship rates (δt\delta_t and βt\beta_t), with weights given by the poverty headcount:

𝐈𝐭=𝐏𝐭𝛅𝐭+(𝟏−𝐏𝐭)𝛃𝐭 \boxed{\boldsymbol{I_t = {\color{maroon}P_t}\,\delta_t + (1-{\color{maroon}P_t})\,\beta_t}}

  • Let PtP_t be the poverty headcount (gross consumption) measure, δt=Pr⁡(m>0∣x<zt)\delta_t=\Pr(m>0\mid x<z_t) the share of the poor with positive OOP and βt=Pr⁡(x−m<zt∣x≥zt)\beta_t=\Pr(x-m<z_t\mid x\ge z_t) the share of the non‑poor pushed below the line.
  • δt\delta_t and βt\beta_t describe how impoverishment is measured for the further pushed and the pushed, respectively.

Combined effects in impoverishment dynamics

Mechanical poverty effect

  • If δ\delta and β\beta are frozen, a fall in PP lowers II by (δ−β)ΔP(\delta-\beta)\,\Delta P. With δ≈0.7\delta\approx0.7 and β≈0.03\beta\approx0.03, each percentage point of poverty reduction removes about 0.65 points of impoverishment — without any change in health financing.

Increased access effect

  • Increased service utilization can translate into increased health OOP at the point of use, δ\delta rises and II rises.
  • A health system that reaches more poor people with partially subsidized care can mean worsening ItI_t (even though welfare could be higher with less foregone care).

Total impoverishment: 𝐈𝐭=𝐏𝐭𝛅𝐭+(𝟏−𝐏𝐭)𝛃𝐭\boxed{\boldsymbol{I_t = {\color{maroon}P_t}\,\delta_t + (1-{\color{maroon}P_t})\,\beta_t}}

  • A clean separation of ΔP\Delta P from (Δδ,Δβ)(\Delta\delta,\Delta\beta) is therefore needed to interpret trends.

Complete decomposition

Factor decomposition – Macro form

Two‑factor Shapley decomposition

  • If we focus now on the decomposition of changes in impoverishment, we could express it as:
ΔI\Delta I == (δ‾−β‾)ΔP(\bar\delta-\bar\beta)\,\Delta P ++ P‾Δδ\bar P\,\Delta\delta ++ (1−P‾)Δβ(1-\bar P)\,\Delta\beta
change in impoverishment poverty component
ΔP\Delta P: change in poverty rate		 FP among the poor
Δδ\Delta\delta: change in FP among the poor (further pushed)		 FP among the non‑poor
Δβ\Delta\beta: change in FP among the non‑poor (pushed)
  • A bar denotes the mid‑point of the two periods: P‾=12(P0+P1)\bar P=\tfrac12(P_0+P_1), δ‾=12(δ0+δ1)\;\bar\delta=\tfrac12(\delta_0+\delta_1), β‾=12(β0+β1)\;\bar\beta=\tfrac12(\beta_0+\beta_1).

Properties

  • Full decomposition: the three terms sum to ΔI\Delta I with zero residual.
  • Symmetric. Two‑factor Shapley value (Shorrocks 2013). Coincides with the average of the two sequential (Oaxaca‑type) decompositions; it is the analogue of Datt and Ravallion (1992) and Kakwani (2000) for impoverishment.
  • Additive across countries: with population weights ωct\omega_{ct}, ΔIW=∑cΔωcI‾c+∑cω‾cΔIc\Delta I_W=\sum_c\Delta\omega_c\bar I_c+\sum_c\bar\omega_c\Delta I_c, and each ΔIc\Delta I_c splits as above.

Illustration with the 2025 GMR global figures (2000 → 2022)

P: 42.6% → 25.1%; 𝛅\boldsymbol{\delta}: 62.4% → 73.9%; 𝛃\boldsymbol{\beta}: 4.0% → 2.5%; I: 28.9% → 20.4%. Poverty component (δ‾−β‾)ΔP=(0.682−0.033)×(−17.5)=−11.4(\bar\delta-\bar\beta)\,\Delta P=(0.682-0.033)\times(-17.5)=-11.4 pp; FP among the poor P‾Δδ=0.339×11.5=+3.9\bar P\,\Delta\delta=0.339\times11.5=+3.9 pp; FP among the non‑poor (1−P‾)Δβ=0.661×(−1.5)=−1.0(1-\bar P)\,\Delta\beta=0.661\times(-1.5)=-1.0 pp; total −8.5-8.5 pp.

Summary

  • Poverty reduction more than explains the decline: on its own it would have lowered impoverishing OOP by 11.4 pp, against 8.5 pp observed (134% of the change).
  • The financial‑protection component contributes against the decrease in total impoverishment (so financial hardship increases and dampens the effect of poverty reduction): among the poor, the probability of paying something out of pocket rose, from 62% to 74% (+3.9 pp). This is consistent with expanded utilisation with incomplete coverage, and with the rise of the large OOP component in middle‑income countries.
  • Among the non‑poor, fewer were pushed below the line: 4.0% → 2.5% (−1.0 pp). Part of this fall can be mechanical, since fewer people live just above the line when poverty falls.

Implementation (i): global estimates from country‑level datapoints

Aggregate data (global estimates)

Object Source Notes
PctP_{ct} poverty headcount at zz WHO–WB UHC GMR: reconstructed poverty headcount for country cc in year tt Reconstructed to align the welfare aggregate (gross of OOP) with the one used for financial hardship
BctB_{ct} further pushed WHO–WB UHC GMR Country‑year, survey years and modelled
ActA_{ct} pushed into poverty WHO–WB UHC GMR Country‑year, survey years and modelled
ωct\omega_{ct} population UN World Population Prospects For world and regional aggregates
  • Calibration of parameters (conditional rates): δct=Bct/Pct\delta_{ct}=B_{ct}/P_{ct} and βct=Act/(1−Pct)\beta_{ct}=A_{ct}/(1-P_{ct}).
    • δct\delta_{ct}: among the poor of country cc in year tt, the share who paid anything out of pocket (the further pushed, divided by the poor).
    • βct\beta_{ct}: among the non‑poor, the share whose OOP took them below the line (the pushed, divided by the non‑poor).
    • All three come from the same surveys, so Bct≤PctB_{ct}\le P_{ct} and the identity holds exactly for each country‑year.
  • Steps
    1. Build a country panel at survey years.
    2. Compute the three components for each country between first and last survey (or between fixed years using the modelled series, flagged).
    3. Aggregate using population weights ωct\omega_{ct}.
    4. Report at global and by region and income group.

Implementation (ii): household survey microdata

(a) Two repeated cross‑sections: simple approach, direct distributions

Two surveys of the same country, at t0t_0 and t1t_1 (different households). For each household: consumption xix_i (gross of OOP), OOP mim_i, the poverty line ztz_t and a sampling weight.

  1. Flag every household in each survey: poor if xi<ztx_i<z_t; further pushed if poor and mi>0m_i>0; pushed if non‑poor and xi−mi<ztx_i-m_i<z_t.
  2. Compute three weighted shares in each survey: PtP_t, the share who are poor; δt\delta_t, the share of the poor who pay something out of pocket; βt\beta_t, the share of the non‑poor pushed below the line. Check that Ptδt+(1−Pt)βtP_t\delta_t+(1-P_t)\beta_t gives back the impoverishment rate ItI_t.
  3. Plug these six numbers into the same formula as for the global figures:
ΔI\Delta I == (δ‾−β‾)ΔP(\bar\delta-\bar\beta)\,\Delta P ++ P‾Δδ\bar P\,\Delta\delta ++ (1−P‾)Δβ(1-\bar P)\,\Delta\beta
change in impoverishment poverty component FP among the poor FP among the non‑poor

Standard errors: bootstrap over PSUs within strata, repeating steps 1–3 in each replicate.

(b) Two repeated cross‑sections: simulated approach (change one dimension at a time)

Impoverishment combines two distributions: Consumption (who is poor) and who pays, and how much (OOP as a share of consumption, mi/xim_i/x_i, at each consumption percentile). With microdata we can simulate them:

OOP pattern of t0t_0 OOP pattern of t1t_1
Consumption of t0t_0 I00I_{00} observed I01I_{01} simulated
Consumption of t1t_1 I10I_{10} simulated I11I_{11} observed
  • Building the simulated distributions: rank households by consumption in each survey; give each t1t_1 household the OOP shares of t0t_0 households in the same percentile, and count who is impoverished (I10I_{10}); I01I_{01} is the other distribution.
  • Poverty component: what happens when only consumption changes, 12[(I10−I00)+(I11−I01)]\tfrac12[(I_{10}-I_{00})+(I_{11}-I_{01})].
  • Financial‑protection component: what happens when only the OOP pattern changes, 12[(I01−I00)+(I11−I10)]\tfrac12[(I_{01}-I_{00})+(I_{11}-I_{10})].
  • Both should add up exactly to ΔI=I11−I00\Delta I=I_{11}-I_{00}. Unlike the previous application, the poverty component also captures changes in who is poor and how many live just above the line.

(c) Two panel waves: follow the same households

The same households are interviewed at t0t_0 and t1t_1. Both cross‑section methods still apply to each wave; the panel adds who moved in and out of impoverishment, and through which channel. Give each household one of four statuses in each wave and cross‑tabulate them (panel weights, % of population):

Status at t0t_0 ↓\downarrow / at t1t_1 →\rightarrow i ii iii iv
i poor, pays OOP (further pushed) · exit, FP · exit, poverty
ii poor, no OOP entry, FP · entry, poverty ·
iii non‑poor, pushed below the line (pushed) · exit, poverty · exit, FP
iv non‑poor, not pushed entry, poverty · entry, FP ·
  • i and iii are impoverished; · means no change in impoverishment status.
  • Poverty channel: the household left or fell into poverty.
  • FP channel: same poverty status, but it started or stopped paying OOP.
  • ΔI\Delta I = entries − exits = poverty channel + FP channel.
  • Panel data: does paying OOP at t0t_0 make it harder to leave poverty, or easier to fall into it, by t1t_1? Compare payers and non‑payers with similar consumption at t0t_0.
